conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m Claire, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-item questionnaire that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling during these first weeks of motherhood. Everything you share stays between us unless there’s an immediate safety concern, and there are no “right” answers—only your honest experience. I’ll ask each question conversationally; just tell me what feels true for you. When you’re ready, we’ll begin.

In the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? I can still laugh when something’s genuinely funny—maybe a cute thing the baby does or a silly text from my best friend—but it feels muted, like I have to remind myself to let it out. It doesn’t come as easily or feel as good as it used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most of the time I can still laugh, but it’s kind of forced—like I’m going through the motions. I’ll chuckle if my husband cracks a joke, yet it fades fast and I’m right back to feeling flat.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to little things—like taking the baby for a short walk or having my mom drop by—but the excitement feels kind of dulled. It’s more “that’ll be nice” than the bubbly can’t-wait feeling I used to get.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. Like yesterday the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset his tummy, or I didn’t burp him long enough. Rationally I know babies just cry, but the thought still pops in that I must’ve messed up somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A few nights this week I’ve lain in bed with my heart racing, running through all the “what-ifs” about the baby—like whether he’s breathing when he’s been quiet too long, or if that tiny cough means he’s getting sick. Nothing’s actually wrong, but I can’t switch the worry off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full-on panicky, but sometimes when he’s napping I’ll suddenly feel this wave of “what if he stops breathing?” and my chest gets tight. It passes if I go peek at him, but it’s like my body’s on alert for no real reason.
Things have been getting on top of me
Yeah… some days it feels like the diapers and feedings and laundry just pile up faster than I can handle them. I’m managing, but by evening I’m wiped and feel like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s not every night, but a couple of times this week I’ve felt kind of heavy and teary once the lights are off, and then I just lie there listening to every little grunt the baby makes. I eventually drift off, but it takes way longer than it should.
I have felt sad or miserable

I get waves of sadness a few times a day—like when I’m rocking the baby and suddenly feel lonely or when I see other moms who look like they’ve got it all together. It’s not constant, but it keeps popping up.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I haven’t actually cried much—maybe once or twice when I was really tired and the baby wouldn’t settle. It’s more like my eyes sting and I feel on the verge, but I usually blink it away before the tears fall.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and tired, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 16: Screening Summary – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh-based self-report; responses reviewed in interview.

Areas endorsed above perinatal norm:  
- Anhedonia: diminished pleasure/enthusiasm (Q2)  
- Dysregulated mood: recurrent waves of sadness, “heavy and teary” evenings (Q8, Q9)  
- Heightened anxiety: nocturnal heart racing, intrusive “what-ifs” re infant safety (Q4, Q5)  
- Guilt/self-blame: attributes infant fussiness to maternal error (Q3)  
- Overwhelm: daily tasks “pile up,” evening exhaustion (Q6)  
- Sleep-onset delay linked to low mood and hyper-vigilance to infant sounds (Q7)  
- Reduced spontaneous laughter, described as “forced” (Q1)

Positive findings:  
- No suicidal ideation or self-harm thoughts (Q10)  
- Able to maintain basic infant care and some social engagement

Screening significance:  
Pattern consistent with mild-to-moderate perinatal depression with comorbid anxiety features. No acute safety concerns identified today; continue monitoring and consider formal assessment (PHQ-9, GAD-7) and/or referral for perinatal mental health services.
